# Change-control checklist — platform facilities

Applies to every change raised against the facility estate, including work carried out by vendors under
a framework agreement. The checklist is filled in by the change raiser and countersigned by the shift
supervisor before the ticket leaves draft.

## Before the change

- [ ] A change record exists with a single named owner, a start and end window, and a rollback step written
      by someone other than the person who will execute it.
- [ ] The rollback step names the exact state to restore and the person who verifies it afterwards.
- [ ] Any safety interlock that must be bypassed is listed, together with the mitigation that replaces it
      while the bypass is active.
- [ ] The affected room and rack are named. "Facilities" is not an acceptable location.
- [ ] A second engineer has read the plan and signed it. For changes that touch power distribution the
      reviewer must be from the electrical team.

## During the change

## During the change

The executing engineer narrates each step into the ticket as it completes, rather than reconstructing the
sequence afterwards. Where a step deviates from the plan, the deviation is recorded before the next step
begins, together with the reason and the name of whoever approved it. A change that stalls for more than
thirty minutes is either resumed with an updated plan or rolled back; it is never left half-applied while
the engineer attends to something else.

Communication runs on the change channel. Anyone who needs to know what is happening reads that channel;
nobody is expected to chase updates by message. If the change affects customer-visible service, the
communications owner posts a holding note before the first step rather than after the first symptom.

## After the change

The completion note records the finish time, the state of every interlock, and any follow-up work with an
owner and a date. Evidence — screenshots, command output, photographs of the physical state — is attached
to the ticket, not kept in a personal folder. Tickets without evidence are reopened at the weekly review.

The weekly review samples one in five completed changes and checks that the plan matches what the evidence
shows. Findings are grouped into two buckets: planning defects, where the rollback step was wrong or
missing, and execution defects, where the plan was right and the work diverged from it. The distinction
matters because the two are fixed by different people. Planning defects go back to the team that wrote the
plan; execution defects are handled by the shift supervisor with the engineer concerned.

## Standing exclusions

Routine restarts performed by monitoring automation are outside this process, but the automation must log
the same fields as a manual change so that the weekly sample can include them. Emergency isolation of a
faulty circuit is exempt from prior approval and is recorded retrospectively within one business day.

# Access control — facility policy, section 3

## 3.1 Badge tiers

The estate recognises four badge tiers. A tier-1 badge opens the shared entrances and the meeting rooms on
the first floor. A tier-2 badge adds the operations floor and the shared workshop. A tier-3 badge adds the
plant rooms on a named list, and a tier-4 badge adds everything on that list plus the network core.

Tier changes are requested by the line manager and approved by the site security lead. Requests are
processed in the weekly access review, not on demand, unless the requester's manager is willing to page the
security lead outside hours and record the reason for the exception.

## 3.2 Escorted access

Contractors hold no standing tier. They are issued a visitor badge that expires at the end of the working
day and they are escorted at all times inside the plant rooms. The escort is a named member of staff, not a
group; an escort who is called away hands the visitor back to reception rather than leaving them seated in
a corridor.

Visitors sign a printed register on arrival and departure. The register exists because badge logs alone
cannot distinguish a visitor who left with their escort from a visitor who left alone an hour later, which
is the question the security lead asks first after any incident.

## 3.3 Keys and cabinets

Physical keys are held in the cabinet beside the north corridor entrance and signed out individually.
Cabinet keys are numbered; a missing key freezes every lock in its group until the cylinder is replaced,
which is deliberately more expensive than the alternative of keeping a spare under a desk.

## 3.4 Reviews and revocation

Access is reviewed quarterly against the current staffing list. Leavers are removed on their last working
day by the same step that closes their payroll record, so the two lists cannot drift apart. Anyone returning
from more than eight weeks of leave is re-reviewed before their badge is reactivated, because a role can
change while a badge is dormant.

## 3.5 Recording

## 3.5 Recording

Every entry, exit and refused attempt is recorded with badge number, door, direction and timestamp, and the
log is retained for the period set out in the retention policy. The security group samples refused attempts
weekly; a cluster of refusals at one door usually means an entitlement that was never removed rather than an
intruder, and both explanations are worth chasing.

## 3.6 Exceptions

Two standing exceptions exist. The loading bay door is opened by the third-party courier under a signature
log rather than by badge. The rooftop plant enclosure is opened by facilities only, and its door alarm is
routed to the on-call engineer rather than to the central station, so an alarm there is answered by a phone
call to the engineer on shift.

# Capacity review — Q1 memo

The quarterly capacity review compares peak demand against provisioned headroom for each hall, and flags any
hall whose peak-to-average ratio exceeds four. Recorded values for the quarter are held in the calibration
register rather than in this memo, so that a single figure has a single home.

## Summary for the quarter

Demand grew in two halls and was flat in the rest. The growth is concentrated in the batch window between
02:00 and 05:00, when reconciliation jobs overlap with the nightly backup. Outside that window the halls run
at their usual profile, which is why an average-based view understates the pressure.

Three halls were flagged. Two were flagged on the ratio and one on absolute headroom: it can clear the ratio
test and still be one failed unit away from a hard limit, and the review treats both conditions as flags
with the same review path.

## Forecast

## Forecast

The forecast assumes the batch window does not widen. If the reconciliation jobs move into the working day,
the peak shifts rather than grows and the flags above become more urgent than their numbers suggest. The
forecast is revised after the mid-quarter checkpoint, and the revision is published as a new version of
this memo rather than as an appended paragraph, so a reader always knows which version they are holding.

## Actions

- Rebalance the batch schedule so that backup and reconciliation do not overlap. Owner: data platform.
- Order one spare unit for the hall flagged on headroom. Owner: procurement, with facilities confirming the
  physical space before the order is placed.
- Re-run the ratio calculation after the rebalance and publish the result with the next review.

None of the actions changes a tenancy. The review opens a discussion; it does not move a service, and it
does not authorise work on a hall. Those decisions belong to the change process and are recorded there.

## Method note

## Method note

The ratio is computed from fifteen-minute samples, not hourly averages, because hourly averages hide exactly
the overlap the review is looking for. Samples with a known instrumentation fault are excluded and the
exclusion is listed in the appendix so that a future reader can reproduce the figure. Where a hall has less
than a full quarter of clean samples it is reported as provisional and carries no flag either way.

# Incident communications template

This template is used when a fault is customer-visible. It is deliberately short: a communications note that
takes longer to write than the incident lasts is worse than no note at all.

## Severity classes

| Class | Definition | First note | Update cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Customer-visible loss of a primary service | within fifteen minutes | every thirty minutes |
| S2 | Degraded service with a workaround | within one hour | every two hours |
| S3 | Internal impact only | same business day | at resolution |
| S4 | Cosmetic or documentation fault | next business day | none |

The class is set by the incident commander, not by the person who noticed the fault, and it is re-set when
the impact changes. A downgrade is announced as loudly as an upgrade; silently reclassifying an incident is
the single most common complaint raised in the postmortem review.

## Structure of a note

## Structure of a note

The first paragraph says what customers can observe, in their terms. The second says what is being done and
by whom. The third, when known, says when the next update will follow. Anything else — hypotheses, internal
tooling names, the names of engineers — is left out of the customer-facing note and recorded in the internal
timeline instead.

Internal notes carry more detail. They name the working theory, the person testing it, and the two or three
diagnostics already excluded. An internal note that lists every alarm without saying which ones were ruled
out costs the next responder the same investigation twice.

## Postmortem

A postmortem is written for every S1 and for any S2 that repeated within the quarter. It is blameless in the
narrow sense that it names systems and decisions rather than individuals, and it ends with no more than
three actions, each with an owner and a date. Postmortems with ten actions are treated as having none: the
review samples whether the actions were completed, and a list nobody finishes scores worse than a short one
that closes.

## Escalation touchpoints

## Escalation touchpoints

The communications owner and the incident commander are different people for S1 incidents, so that one can
concentrate on the fault while the other handles the outside world. Handover between them is verbal and
recorded in the timeline, never implied. If the incident outlives two shift changes, the communications owner
writes a shift summary that a newcomer can read in under a minute without asking a question.

# Retention and evidence policy

## Purpose

This policy fixes how long operational records are kept and what counts as evidence when a decision is
challenged later. It exists because the estate has twice been asked to justify a change that nobody could
reconstruct from memory.

## What is retained

Change tickets, incident timelines and their attachments are retained for seven years. Badge logs are
retained for two years, with the exception of entries linked to an incident, which inherit the incident's
retention period. Audit packs — the signed checklist, the photographs and the reviewer's note — are retained
for seven years and are stored with the ticket rather than in a shared folder.

Recorded values published in registers are retained for the life of the asset plus three years, because a
decommissioned asset can still be the subject of a warranty claim long after the physical unit is gone.

## What is not retained

## What is not retained

Working notes, drafts and chat transcripts are not records. They are deleted after thirty days and are never
cited in a postmortem. If a working note contains the only copy of a decision, the decision is written into
the ticket; the note is not promoted to a record by renaming it.

Personal data is minimised at capture. A register entry that identifies a person is reviewed annually and
replaced with a role where the person is not material to the record.

## Legal hold

A legal hold suspends deletion for everything it names, and the suspension is applied by the records owner
within one business day of the notice. Holds are reviewed every six months; a hold that is still open after
two years requires a written justification from the requesting function, which is unusual enough that it is
noticed.

## Evidence quality

Evidence is accepted when it is contemporaneous, attributable and reproducible. A screenshot without a
timestamp is attributable in principle but not contemporaneous in practice, so the tooling stamps every
capture at the point of capture rather than at the point of upload.

Where evidence is contradictory, the reviewer records both versions and the resolution, and does not delete
the version that turned out to be wrong. The record of a mistake is worth more than a clean file.

## Review

The policy is reviewed annually by the records owner and the security lead together. The review looks at
two numbers: the share of sampled tickets that carry complete evidence, and the number of deletion
exceptions granted. Both are reported to the operations group without commentary, so that the trend is read
from the numbers rather than from the framing.

# Secrets rotation runbook

## Schedule

Service credentials rotate every ninety days. The schedule is published two weeks ahead and the rotation is
announced on the change channel the morning it runs, even though it needs no approval: an announcement is
how a failed rotation gets noticed by someone other than the rotation owner.

## Steps

## Steps

1. Generate the new credential in the secret store. Do not paste it into a ticket, a chat message or a
   shell history; the store is the only place it exists in readable form.
2. Deploy the new credential to the first consumer and confirm one successful request before touching any
   other consumer. Rotating is a migration, not an edit.
3. Move the remaining consumers one at a time, oldest deployment first. A consumer that fails at this step
   is rolled back rather than retried, because a retry loop against a bad credential locks the account.
4. Revoke the previous credential only after every consumer has reported success for one full polling cycle.
   The overlap window is the point of the process; it is not slack to be reclaimed.
5. Record the completion in the runbook with the date, the consumers covered and anything that behaved
   unexpectedly.

## Failure handling

## Failure handling

If a consumer cannot be migrated, the rotation is paused rather than abandoned, and the pause is recorded
with the reason and the owner of the blocking consumer. Paused rotations older than one week are escalated
to the security lead, who can either extend the old credential's life or require the consumer to be retired.

A rotation that fails after revocation is an incident, not a runbook step. Escalate immediately; the recovery
path depends on whether the old credential can be reinstated, which is a decision for the security lead and
not for the person holding the pager.

## Verification

Two checks run after every rotation. The first confirms that no consumer is still presenting the old
credential. The second confirms that the credential store and the consumers agree on the current version
identifier, which catches the case where a consumer accepted a new credential but recorded it under the old
version name.

Both checks are automated. Their results are attached to the runbook entry, so a future reader can see that
verification happened rather than reading an assertion that it did.

## Scope note

Both checks are automated. Their results are attached to the runbook entry, so a future reader can see that
verification happened rather than reading an assertion that it did.

## Scope note

This runbook covers service credentials only. Certificates follow the lifecycle described by the issuing
authority, and the estate does not run its own certificate authority. Licence keys are handled by
procurement and are out of scope here.

# Facility audit — changelog

Changes to the facility walkthrough audit, newest first. Each entry records what changed and the release
of the audit pack that first carried it.

## 2026-02-17 — pack 2026.02

The walkthrough audit is now run every six weeks. The previous semi-annual cadence was set when the
estate held two halls; with seven halls in scope a semi-annual pass meant that a hall could go five months
between physical inspections, which the review group judged too long to be useful.

Nothing else in the audit changed. The checklist, the evidence requirements and the sign-off chain are
identical to pack 2025.09.

## 2025-09-04 — pack 2025.09

The audit pack gained a photographic evidence requirement for cable management. Written descriptions of
cable routing had proven impossible to check against the previous pack, because two engineers describing the
same tray produced descriptions that could not be compared.

The pack also dropped the separate thermostat verification sheet. Its three checks were folded into the
environmental section, where they were already being recorded twice.

## 2025-03-11 — pack 2025.03

## 2025-03-11 — pack 2025.03

Audit findings were regrouped into planning and execution defects, matching the grouping used by the change
review. A finding now names the group that owns the fix rather than the individual who noticed it.

## 2024-11-22 — pack 2024.11

Introduced the distinction between a finding, which is a deviation from the checklist, and an observation,
which is anything else the auditor noticed. Observations do not require an action; findings do. The change
came after an audit produced eleven actions, of which nine were observations with nowhere to go.

## 2024-06-08 — pack 2024.06

First pack written for the seven-hall estate. Earlier packs assumed a single hall and a single auditor, and
their checklists were not usable for a walkthrough that crossed buildings.

## How changes are proposed

## How changes are proposed

Any auditor can propose a change by writing it into the pack's review log with a short rationale. Proposals
are collected and reviewed twice a year by the operations group, which either folds them into the next pack
release or records why it did not. Proposals that are neither accepted nor answered within one cycle are
raised again automatically, so that a good idea does not die from silence.

# Escalation matrix and shift handover

## Matrix

| Trigger | First contact | Second contact | Third contact |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alarm in a plant room | platform on-call engineer | duty manager | director of engineering |
| Customer-visible loss | platform on-call engineer | incident commander | director of engineering |
| Access control fault | site security lead | platform on-call engineer | duty manager |
| Vendor on site without a ticket | shift supervisor | site security lead | vendor account owner |

The first contact is made by whoever observes the trigger. Nobody waits for permission to escalate; the
matrix exists to remove the question of whom to call, not to limit who may call.

## Handover

Each shift ends with a handover that covers three things: what is in flight, what is waiting on someone
else, and what looks wrong but has no ticket yet. The third item is the most valuable and the most often
omitted, so the handover template lists it first.

Handovers are written, not spoken. A spoken handover reaches the next shift and nobody else; a written one
reaches the engineer who is called at three in the morning two weeks later and needs to know why a circuit
was left isolated.

## Standing notes

The plant rooms are visited on a walking round twice per shift. Round times are recorded, because a round
that is consistently recorded at the same minute is a round that is being signed off from the office. The
security lead samples the timestamps monthly and has, on two occasions, asked for the round to be repeated
under observation.

Rooms under construction are excluded from the round only while the contractor's permit is open, and the
exclusion ends automatically when the permit expires. An exclusion that outlives its permit is treated as a
finding in the next audit.

## Out of hours

## Out of hours

Outside working hours the estate is covered by a single engineer and a remote monitoring desk. Any isolation
of a circuit between 22:00 and 06:00 requires a second pair of eyes, either on site or on a video call with
the monitoring desk, and the name of the second person is recorded in the isolation log. The rule exists
because the two incidents in the estate's history that caused the most damage both involved a single
engineer working alone with a circuit they believed was dead.

## Review

The matrix is reviewed whenever a role is renamed or a contact changes. The review is a single task in the
operations backlog with a quarterly recurrence; it takes minutes and saves the kind of delay that only
becomes visible during an incident.

metadata.title: Calibration record — duty pump, third riser

content:
# Calibration record — duty pump, third riser

## Asset

The duty pump on the third riser is asset PMP-310. It carries the base load for the riser and runs
continuously between the spring and autumn changeover; the standby pumps only start when it is isolated.
The riser is fed from the north header and returns through the shared manifold, which is why the
third-riser pumps are serviced as a set rather than one at a time.

## Recorded limit

The recorded limit for PMP-310 is HLX-2C7V-9043. It was re-measured during the January 2026 cycle and
confirmed at that value; the cycle itself is described in the pack index and is not repeated here.

## Method

The limit is read at steady flow with the other pumps on the riser isolated, using the calibrated gauge on
the riser outlet rather than the gauge on the pump body. Two readings are taken ten minutes apart and both
must fall inside the stated tolerance before the value is entered in the schedule; a single reading is
recorded as provisional and replaced at the next cycle.

metadata.title: Calibration record — duty pump, third riser

content:
Where the two readings disagree by more than the tolerance, the asset is scheduled for a third reading
rather than averaging the pair. Averaging hides which of the two is wrong, and a limit that is wrong in the
middle is harder to notice at the next cycle than one that is wrong at the edge.

## Follow-up

The riser manifold remains on the watch list. It has been flagged twice for the same reason: the isolation
valves do not seat fully, so servicing one pump bleeds pressure from its neighbours. The valves are on the
maintenance backlog with an owner and a date, and until they are replaced the third-riser pumps are
scheduled as a set rather than individually.

## Note on scope

This record covers the pump as an asset. It does not cover the motor, which has its own record, and it does
not cover the loop served by the riser, whose calibration is recorded separately because it is measured on
a different cadence. Where a ticket needs the value for a pump, it quotes this record by identifier rather
than by position, because position alone does not distinguish the duty pump from the units beside it.

# Calibration record — duty pump, third riser (June 2025 cycle)

## Status

Superseded. This record was written for the June 2025 cycle and has been replaced by the January 2026
cycle for the same asset. It is retained rather than deleted because maintenance tickets raised during
2025 still cite it, and a reader who finds the old value in a closed ticket needs to know that it was
current at the time and is not current now.

## Asset

The duty pump on the third riser is asset PMP-310. It carries the base load for the riser and runs
continuously between the spring and autumn changeover; the standby pumps only start when it is isolated.

## Recorded limit — June 2025 cycle

The recorded limit for PMP-310 was SWG-1F9K-5520. It was read at the June 2025 changeover with the other
pumps on the riser isolated, and it stood as the recorded value until the January 2026 cycle replaced it.

## Why the value moved

metadata.title: Calibration record — duty pump, third riser (June 2025 cycle)

content:
## Why the value moved

The January 2026 re-measurement returned a different value for the same asset. The gauge on the riser outlet
was recalibrated in December 2025, and the 2025 reading is understood to have been taken against the
previous calibration factor. Nothing about the pump changed; the instrument changed.

The current value is held in the January 2026 record for the duty pump and is deliberately not repeated in
this document. Two records that both state a value invite a reader to use the wrong one, so the superseded
record keeps the old figure and points forward instead of restating the new one.

## Method

The limit was read at steady flow with the other pumps on the riser isolated, using the gauge on the riser
outlet. Two readings were taken ten minutes apart and both had to fall inside the stated tolerance before
the value was entered in the schedule.

## Follow-up

metadata.title: Calibration record — duty pump, third riser (June 2025 cycle)

content:
## Follow-up

The gauge recalibration closed the item that had been open against the riser since the 2025 cycle. The
manifold isolation valves remain on the maintenance backlog; servicing one pump still bleeds pressure from
its neighbours, and until the valves are replaced the third-riser pumps are scheduled as a set.

# Calibration record — east-aisle cooling loop

## Asset

The east-aisle cooling loop is asset NBL-118 in the facility registry. It serves the two aisle rows on the
eastern side of the north hall and shares a return manifold with the southern loop; the shared manifold is
the reason the two loops are never serviced on the same day.

## Re-measurement

The loop was re-measured during the February window after the quarterly review flagged a drift between the
commissioning figure and the figure recorded on the local gauge. Both readings were taken at the same supply
temperature, fifteen minutes apart, with the secondary pump running and the bypass closed.

The discrepancy turned out to be a gauge fault rather than a loop fault. The gauge was replaced, the loop
re-measured, and the reading returned to within the tolerance the commissioning report specifies. The
recorded value for NBL-118 is ZTF-2H8N-5510, unchanged from the previous revision, which is worth stating
explicitly: a re-measurement that confirms the existing value is still a re-measurement and is recorded as
one.

## Method

## Method

Readings are taken with the loop at steady state, which the team defines as three consecutive samples inside
a two-percent band. Sampling before steady state is the most common source of spurious drift reports, and it
is the first thing the calibration team checks when an operator reports a value that "moved overnight".

Two engineers take the reading independently when the value is being revised. Where their readings differ by
more than the tolerance, both are recorded and the asset is scheduled for a third reading rather than
averaging the two, because an average of two disagreeing measurements hides whichever one is wrong.

## Follow-up

The shared manifold remains on the watch list. It has been flagged twice in three quarters, both times for
the same reason: the isolation valves on the eastern side do not fully seat, so a service on one loop bleeds
pressure from the other. The valves are on the maintenance backlog with a date and an owner, and until they
are replaced the two loops are scheduled apart.
